officer.body:
Dear Nicci,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since the strategy was set. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy pack taken to Cabinet on 9 February and on to Council on 23 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is clearly written and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The interest-rate assumption behind the £4.8m debt-interest budget on Appendix 1 page 15 is 4.75% for new long-term loans, tied to Arlingclose's rate table on page 18 with a 22 December 2025 date. Since December the long end of the Certainty curve has moved up quite a bit. On yesterday afternoon's fixing 5-year Certainty is around 5.34%, 10-year 5.83%, and 25- and 50-year run 6.46% and 6.27%. Your 4.75% assumption sits about 0.6 of a point below 5-year Certainty and 1.5 or more below anything longer than ten years. The 10-year HRA rate at Gilt + 0.40 works out closer to 5.43% today, so 4.75% stays broadly attainable at short-dated PWLB or an HRA-marked loan — which is what your Borrowing Strategy paragraphs on pages 5 to 7 explicitly point at. Less an issue for the assumption than a sense of how narrow the maturity window is that keeps the budget number honest at today's rates.

The other thing that stood out is the shape of the liability benchmark chart on page 5. Very few LBs we've read this year decay to zero. Most are showing benchmarks that climb into the 2030s and stay there. Yours, on your published forecast, tracks the CFR down as it falls, and by the late 2030s the benchmark has closed on the loan tail; the note beneath the chart explains why some fixed-rate loans keep running past that point, which reads right. Worth flagging as a strength of the book's shape rather than anything to act on. The two-and-three-quarter times ratio between the upper limits on the revenue impact of a 1% rate rise (£345,000) and a 1% fall (£125,000) at Interest rate exposures on page 13 reads consistently with it — the revenue exposure sits on the debt-side refinancing, not on the investment side.

We price every published PWLB book daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. On the point Debt rescheduling makes at page 7 — that the recent rise in rates should surface more favourable rescheduling opportunities than in prior years — that's broadly what we see across the sector today, indicative only, and only the DMO can quote. We should note our own loan file for Canterbury does not currently tie to your Appendix B, which is a data-quality issue on our side we're working on; disclosing it because we'd rather flag it than gloss it, but not asking you to act on it.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central, and an interactive version is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. In your specific case, where the LB decays, the useful thing is probably stress-testing the pace of the decay against variations in the £44m borrowing plan on page 4.

On training, three fit the paper. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice picks up the chart on page 5. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator covers the Debt rescheduling section. MRP — policy options and revenue impact sits behind the CFR trajectory that shapes the benchmark. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Strategy Report, Cabinet 9 February 2026, at https://democracy.canterbury.gov.uk/documents/s132535/treasury-management-strategy-report.pdf, with Appendix 1 (Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27) at .../s132536/ and Appendix 3 (Non-treasury Investment Strategy 2026/27) at .../s132538/.
